title: Effect of Respiratory Rate on Ventilation Distribution Assessed by Electrical Impedance Tomography in Mechanically Ventilated Patients: A Physiological Pilot Study
summary:
What is this study about?
Many critically ill patients in the intensive care unit need to be supported by a breathing machine (a ventilator), because their lungs are temporarily unable to manage breathing on their own. The ventilator then takes over the work of breathing. Several settings can be chosen on such a machine – for example, how many breaths per minute the machine delivers (the so-called respiratory rate) and how much air it pushes into the lungs with each breath (the tidal volume). As helpful as mechanical ventilation is, it can also place strain on the sensitive lung tissue. In recent years, it has become clear that the respiratory rate – that is, how fast a patient is ventilated – may also play a role in how gentle or how stressful ventilation is for the lungs. Yet surprisingly little is known about which respiratory rate is the most favourable.

What do we want to find out?
We want to understand whether ventilation works equally well across the full range of respiratory rates commonly used in everyday practice – or whether, with certain settings, the air is distributed more unevenly within the lungs. An even distribution of air throughout the entire lung is important so that all regions take part in gas exchange and the lung is protected.

How will we do this?
To make the distribution of air in the lungs visible, we use a method called electrical impedance tomography. A belt with measuring points is placed around the chest, which can show from the outside which areas of the lung the air flows into. The method is completely painless, uses no X-rays, and is also used in routine intensive care.
During the study, the respiratory rate on the ventilator is changed step by step, while the other settings remain unchanged. This is done in two runs, each with a different tidal volume, so that the two situations can be compared. Which of the two runs comes first is decided at random. Each participant goes through both variants and therefore serves, in a sense, as their own comparison. At defined time points, small blood samples are also taken to check how well gas exchange – that is, the uptake of oxygen and the release of carbon dioxide – is functioning.

What does taking part mean for patients?
All the adjusted settings remain within the range that is also customary in routine intensive care. Throughout the entire examination, patients are monitored particularly closely. Should certain predefined limit values be reached, the examination is stopped immediately.

interventions.name:
Intra-individual crossover design, in which all patients undergo two protocols in succession in randomised order.

In Protocol A, titration is performed in steps of 4 breaths/min each, beginning at a respiratory rate of 12/min up to 28/min. The tidal volume is fixed at 6 ml/kg ideal body weight (I
In Protocol B, titration is performed in steps of 3 breaths/min each, from 9 to 21/min, with the tidal volume fixed at 8 ml/kg IBW and the I:E ratio likewise fixed at 1:1.5.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Mechanical ventilation in intensive care unit
Exclusion criteria:
Risk of raised intracranial pressure, pregnancy, electrically active implants (pacemakers, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators), unstable spinal or thoracic injuries, BMI > 50, open skin lesions in the area of the electrode positions, drains or dressings that make correct electrode positioning impossible.
